problems.description: init_db() was moved from the __main__ guard to module scope (app.py), creating an import-time side effect: importing app (e.g. by a test runner or a later session) initializes/creates tasks.db in the CWD even when no server is started. The tests compensate via monkeypatch + explicit init_db(), but a stray DB file can be created on import.

test_create_task_blank_title asserts 400 for whitespace title, but no whitespace/blank-title validation appears in the app.py diff (only missing-title handling is visible); '   ' is truthy so a 'if not title' check would not reject it. If validation is absent, this test fails; unverifiable from the diff alone.

Most measured convention violations (6 of 8) cite files NOT in this diff (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py), and the app.py/test_app.py 'PascalCase' hits are on files where no classes were added. The 0.73 score appears to reflect the whole worktree, not this commit's changes, which are themselves clean.

strengths: Removed dead code and legacy cruft (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin stub, fetch_task alias), net-reducing technical debt
Fixed a real seed bug: new tasks default status 'done' → 'pending'
Comprehensive test suite (11 tests) covering happy paths, ordering, and error cases with proper isolation (tmp_path + monkeypatch DATABASE)
Preserved the seed's section structure (Models/Routes), snake_case naming, type hints, and error-handling shape
Docstring contract updated to accurately describe the API surface
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, de-leveraging greenfield session that fixes a seed bug and adds solid test coverage while preserving the seed's structure, though the module-scoped init_db() introduces a minor import-time side effect and the measured 0.73 convention score mostly reflects violations in files outside this commit.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT (base64 + hmac) instead of a battle-tested library like PyJWT; custom token code is an easy source of subtle signing/parsing vulnerabilities.
Insecure default SECRET_KEY ('dev-secret-key-change-me') is used when SECRET_KEY env is unset, making tokens trivially forgeable in any deployment that forgets to set it.
Migration adds owner_id as NULL for pre-existing rows, but all read/write paths now filter on owner_id, orphaning legacy tasks so no user can see or update them.
No index on tasks.owner_id; per-user queries ('WHERE owner_id = ?') will full-scan as the table grows.

Convention score 0.73 with 8 violations; several (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, test_app.py) are in files outside this commit's diff and are likely pre-existing, while the app.py 'PascalCase class' finding is not visible in the added diff.

strengths: Passwords hashed via werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash, never stored plaintext.
Timing-safe signature verification via hmac.compare_digest.
Row-level ownership scoping applied consistently to all task reads and writes, plus exp/iat claims in the token.
Additive, backward-compatible migration preserved in init_db rather than a destructive reset.
Clean use of flask.g and functools.wraps in the auth decorator, consistent with the existing get_db/init_db storage pattern.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid feature-addition session that layers in per-user JWT auth with proper hashing and ownership scoping, but hand-rolls token crypto and ships an insecure default secret.

problems.description: Notification dispatch (send_notification_email.delay) is inlined in the edit_task controller; if the Celery broker is unreachable, .delay() can raise on the request path after a successful DB update, leaving the API to 500 while the task was already updated. Consider a try/except or a thin service seam.
get_user_by_id duplicates the fetchone()-pattern of the existing get_user_by_username; a shared _get_user_by(query, params) helper would avoid the copy.

Mechanical convention score (0.73) is dragged down by likely static-analysis false positives (PascalCase flagged on the celery_app instance, snake_case flagged on snake_case functions) and one file not in this diff (repositories.py); actual code follows PEP8 and existing naming.

Adding Celery introduces a new runtime dependency (Redis broker); appropriate here since the story targets a Celery-based app, but the notification feature assumes the broker/worker are running for the app to behave as designed.

strengths: Notification is only dispatched on a genuine status transition to completed (previous_status captured before update), with tests guarding both non-completed and already-completed paths.
The email-column migration mirrors the existing owner_id ALTER TABLE pattern in init_db, including a pragmatic backfill.
Clean module separation (celery_app.py / celery_config.py) with task_routes declared and env-overridable broker/backend config.
Strong test coverage: task unit test, trigger/no-trigger/no-retrigger behavior via monkeypatched delay, plus a config assertion.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, pattern-consistent integration of async email notifications that fits the story's Celery-based architecture, with only minor coupling and duplication worth noting.

problems.description: The refactor removes all module-level data-access functions from app.py and adds a 151-line repositories.py, but no test file was updated (+1 file only). If test_app.py imports the old functions (create_user, get_task, etc.) directly it will break; at minimum the new repository layer has zero dedicated coverage.

BaseRepository uses f-string interpolation for the table name ("SELECT * FROM {self.table_name}") instead of a parameterized identifier. Not exploitable today because table_name is a hardcoded class attribute, but it is a fragile pattern that becomes an injection risk if subclasses ever derive the name from input.

repositories.py introduces a new module-level constant naming violation (lint: Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE), one of the 8 violations; the other 7 are pre-existing in files untouched by this commit.
class attribute declared as `table_name: str = None` — the annotation says str while the value is None; should be `str | None` or a concrete default.

Inconsistent method naming across repositories (find_by_id/find_by_owner/find_by_id_and_owner vs create_user/create_task/update_task), and BaseRepository is an ABC that nevertheless holds concrete CRUD implementations, blurring the abstract/concrete boundary.

strengths: Clean application of the Repository pattern — route handlers no longer touch SQL, improving separation of concerns.
Correct dependency direction: app.py imports repositories (no circular import); repositories.py depends only on werkzeug.security.
Behavior-preserving refactor: owner-scoping is retained via find_by_id_and_owner and find_by_owner, and the removed imports (generate_password_hash, datetime) are relocated to the new module.
Injects the connection factory (get_db) into repositories instead of scattering per-call connections.
Net line reduction (-101) with duplicated query logic consolidated into a reusable base CRUD implementation.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound, behavior-preserving Repository-pattern refactor that encapsulates data access and removes SQL from route handlers — a net architectural improvement — but it ships without accompanying tests and introduces a few minor conventions/robustness warts (f-string table name, stray type annotation, one new lint violation) that should be cleaned up.

problems.description: find_by_owner_paginated keyset orders by id DESC, silently changing the documented GET /tasks contract ('created_at desc'); the two orderings diverge if created_at is ever set explicitly, and cursor stability depends on the id monotonicity assumption.

Every paginated page runs a COUNT(*) over the full owner row set in addition to the page query (O(n) per request); acceptable for this app but scales poorly and could be hoisted or dropped in favor of the cursor-only contract.

The app now hard-depends on a Redis instance (RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI default redis://localhost:6379/0) at import time for the global Limiter; if Redis is down the API fails on the cross-cutting path, not just on rate-limited routes.

All 8 measured convention violations (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE module constants in app.py/celery_app.py/celery_config.py/repositories.py/test_app.py) are pre-existing and in lines/files untouched by this diff — the commit introduces none of them.

GET /tasks response shape changes from a bare list to {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking API change, but consistent with the story's incremental-build pattern and all affected tests were updated in the same commit.

strengths: Cross-cutting rate limiting is centralized at the app level (Limiter with env-driven config) and keyed per authenticated user via JWT sub, falling back to remote address for unauthenticated endpoints — a sound brute-force mitigation for /auth/login.
Cursor-based (keyset) pagination over OFFSET is efficient and stable under concurrent insert/delete, with a clean {data, next_cursor, total} response contract.

Good test coverage: default limit, full page-walk with id uniqueness + descending order assertion, limit param, cap at 100, and existing tests updated for the new shape; env set before import + memory:// storage + limiter.reset() in the fixture is correct test hygiene.
The repository method follows the existing BaseRepository/_connect/_to_dict pattern, and new code is convention-clean (snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE constants).
commit_reviews.summary: A solid cross-cutting commit (rate limiting + keyset pagination + tests) that respects the existing layered architecture and adds no new convention violations — the 0.73 mechanical convention score reflects pre-existing issues in untouched files, while the diff's own additions are clean.

compounding_issues: Hand-rolled JWT (HMAC-SHA256) from Session 2 persisted as the auth foundation, forcing Session 5's rate-limit key function to re-decode tokens and duplicate the parsing logic in token_required (app.py:154-160 vs 137-148)

The single-file app.py accumulated auth + notification code across Sessions 1-3 (growing to ~340 lines) before Session 4's repository extraction, concentrating technical debt that a later session had to unwind
Async email notification is mocked to stdout (celery_app.py:19) — the 'integration' feature is a skeleton, not real email delivery, and later sessions never upgraded it
The tier1_minimal/bad seed shipped an injected bug (create_task inserted status 'done' but returned 'pending'), which Session 1 had to silently fix inside its greenfield commit
A fresh SQLite connection is opened per repository operation and Celery/rate-limit share the same localhost:6379 Redis (env-configurable but coupled by default)
key_decisions: Hand-rolled HS256 JWT with constant-time signature comparison and exp validation instead of adopting PyJWT — functional but reinvents crypto primitives
Session 4 repository-pattern extraction into repositories.py (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository), cleanly removing all raw SQL from route handlers without behavior change
Celery + Redis broker/backend for async task-completion notifications, with a test-friendly .delay seam that Session 3's tests monkeypatch
Inline PRAGMA-driven ALTER TABLE migrations in init_db() to add owner_id/email to existing databases without data loss
Session 5 cursor-based pagination and per-user Flask-Limiter rate limiting (JWT-subject keyed) built on the Session 2 auth layer
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose steadily across the arc. Test coverage grew monotonically (10 → 19 → 24 → 24 → 33) and code stayed green at every commit, ending with all 33 tests passing and exit code 0 in every session. Session 4's refactor was a pure extraction — it held the test count while shrinking app.py from ~340 to ~230 lines by moving 151 lines into a clean repository layer — demonstrating disciplined restructuring rather than churn. Session 5's cross-cutting features (rate limiting, pagination) deliberately reused the earlier JWT and repository layers rather than bypassing them, and added regression tests for notification dedup, user isolation, and cursor paging. Confidence stayed 1.0 and costs remained modest throughout; the one soft spot is that the hand-rolled JWT and the mock email sink remain as latent maintenance/security risks that no later session addressed.
story_review.summary: A textbook-coherent greenfield→feature→integration→refactor→cross-cutting progression that built features on prior seams, fixed the seed's injected bug, refactored cleanly without regressions, and finished with a fully passing 33-test suite — high coherence with only modest residual technical debt in the hand-rolled JWT and mock email path.
